correctness.rationale: For every integer \(k\ge0\), the four morphic blocks of length \(2^k\) partition the infinite word at aligned positions. The inductive identities \(A_k=B_k+C_k\) coordinatewise and \(D_k=0^{2^k}\) show that every aligned block is coordinatewise dominated by \(A_k\). Any shifted length-\(2^k\) factor lies in two adjacent aligned blocks and is bounded in total weight by a rotation of \(A_k\), so the initial block attains the global maximum. The block-weight recurrence has initial values 1,2 and gives \(F_{k+2}\). Every integer weight between zero and the maximum occurs by the step-at-most-one sliding-window property, since expanding the state \(D\) supplies arbitrarily long zero factors. Monotonicity of maximal weight brackets all lengths between dyadic scales, proving the global Fibonacci exponent. The Baum–Sweet identification is verified using all four transition states and binary-digit recurrences. The included verify.py checks a finite sample from its actual packaged source file; it is not substituted for any infinite proof. No exceptional length or endpoint is omitted.

value.rationale: Abelian complexity counts the possible letter-frequency vectors of factors and is a standard structural invariant in combinatorics on words. The lengths \(2^k\) are canonical substitution scales rather than arbitrary samples. A coordinatewise extremal property over all shifts yields the exact infinite-scale classification \(\psi_b(2^k)=F_{k+2}+1\), and the global asymptotic exponent \(\log_2\varphi\) follows without additional unproved regularity. Arbitrarily long zero blocks distinguish this nonuniformly recurrent automatic word from common linear-growth examples. The finite-sample checker corroborates the proof but is not itself the reason for the value assessment.
